planting.note: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates, or early spring where winters are severe, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; sky lupine seed benefits from scarification or a brief cold-moist period to improve germination.

directions: Direct sow in fall in mild-winter climates, or early spring where winters are severe, into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; sky lupine seed benefits from scarification or a brief cold-moist period to improve germination. Palmately divided, silvery-green leaves and dense spikes of small, sky-blue, pea-shaped flowers with a white or yellow center cover open grasslands and hillsides across California each spring, often blooming in massive drifts alongside California poppy as one of the classic combinations of the state's spring wildflower displays. As a nitrogen-fixing legume, it enriches the soil it grows in, and its extremely showy, reliable bloom makes it a favorite component of California native wildflower seed mixes for meadow and slope plantings. It completes its life cycle in a single cool season and self-sows readily where conditions suit it, requiring no supplemental water or fertilizer once established.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; foothill penstemon needs sharp drainage and struggles in heavy clay or overwatered garden soil.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; foothill penstemon needs sharp drainage and struggles in heavy clay or overwatered garden soil. Narrow, blue-green leaves set off tall spikes of vivid blue to violet-blue, tubular flowers held well above the foliage from late spring through summer, one of the most intensely blue-flowered of the California native penstemons and a strong draw for bees and hummingbirds. Native to dry, rocky foothill slopes and chaparral edges across California, it thrives on lean soil and minimal supplemental water once established, making it a good choice for a California native meadow, rock garden, or dry border. Cut back spent flower spikes to tidy the plant and may encourage a lighter rebloom, and avoid rich, moist soil or heavy mulch that can lead to crown rot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; showy penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, tolerating summer dry periods without supplemental water.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; showy penstemon needs sharp drainage and is drought-tolerant once established, tolerating summer dry periods without supplemental water. Thick, blue-green leaves clasp tall, sturdy flower stalks topped with dense clusters of large, funnel-shaped, violet-blue to lavender-pink flowers in spring, one of the tallest and showiest of the Southern California native penstemons and a favorite of bees and hummingbirds. Native to dry chaparral and coastal sage scrub slopes of Southern California and Baja California, it is a long-lived, drought-tolerant perennial well suited to a xeriscape or native plant border, providing bold vertical structure and color when massed. Cut back spent flower stalks after bloom to tidy the plant, and avoid overwatering or rich soil, which shortens its lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalina California fuchsia is a larger, more vigorous selection that spreads readily once established and tolerates heat and drought well.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Catalina California fuchsia is a larger, more vigorous selection that spreads readily once established and tolerates heat and drought well. Soft, gray-green, felted foliage sets off masses of vivid red-orange, tubular flowers from late summer into fall, a season when few other California natives are still blooming, making it an important late-season nectar source for migrating hummingbirds preparing for their journey south. This robust selection, originating from Catalina Island populations, grows larger and spreads more vigorously by rhizome than many other California fuchsia cultivars, useful for covering a dry slope or bank where a spreading groundcover is wanted. It needs no supplemental water once established and benefits from being cut back hard in late winter to remove old growth before the next season's flush.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Winnifred Gilman sage needs sharp drainage and is more compact and better suited to smaller gardens than the species.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Winnifred Gilman sage needs sharp drainage and is more compact and better suited to smaller gardens than the species. Intensely aromatic, wrinkled gray-green leaves cover a rounded, well-branched shrub topped with dense whorls of vivid violet-blue flowers held on distinctive purple-black flower stalks, a strong color contrast that makes this one of the most popular selections of Cleveland sage grown in California native gardens. Its compact size compared to the straight species, combined with exceptional fragrance and a long bloom season that draws bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, makes it a standout choice for a sunny xeriscape border or native pollinator garden. It needs no supplemental water once established and resents rich soil, heavy mulch, or summer irrigation, all of which shorten its naturally long lifespan.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ray Hartman ceanothus needs excellent drainage above all else and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Ray Hartman ceanothus needs excellent drainage above all else and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot. A vigorous, large-growing hybrid between two California native ceanothus species, it produces masses of medium-blue flower clusters over glossy, deep green foliage in early spring, growing quickly into a substantial evergreen shrub or small multi-trunked tree that can be trained with a single leader for a more tree-like form. One of the most reliable and widely planted ceanothus hybrids in California native gardens, it tolerates poor soil and heat with essentially no supplemental water once established, and its abundant spring bloom is a major early-season draw for native bees. Water only during the first year or two of establishment, then withhold summer irrigation entirely, and prune lightly after flowering if shaping is needed.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Howard McMinn manzanita needs excellent drainage and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Howard McMinn manzanita needs excellent drainage and is intolerant of summer irrigation once established, which promotes root rot. Smooth, deep mahogany-red bark and glossy, rounded evergreen leaves cover a dense, mounding shrub topped with small clusters of pink-tinged white, urn-shaped flowers in late winter that are an important early nectar source for native bees and hummingbirds, followed by small berry-like fruit favored by birds. One of the most widely planted and reliably garden-tolerant manzanita cultivars, valued for its adaptability to a wider range of garden conditions than many finickier manzanita species while retaining the group's signature smooth red bark and drought tolerance. Water only during the first year or two of establishment, then rely on natural rainfall alone, and avoid summer water, rich soil, and heavy mulch piled against the trunk, all of which shorten the plant's life.
